historyReviewBoundary: All 115 histories have author source checks. Final independent review covered metadata and numerical checks for all 115 classes, 12 deeper class targets and source-gap samples in seven classes. It did not independently verify every passage of every cited source.

history.name: P2Y12 platelet inhibitors

starting.description: An anti-inflammatory analogue program based on tinoridine yielded an unexpected antiplatelet and antithrombotic effect in orally dosed rats; investigators developed ticlopidine and analogues. A separate P2T antagonist program built on the known competitive antagonist activity of ATP by developing ATP analogues.

inspiration.description: Unexpected animal antiplatelet and antithrombotic effects of synthetic thienopyridines supplied the ticlopidine-to-clopidogrel lead. A separate program built ATP analogues from the observed activity of the endogenous nucleotide as a weak P2T antagonist.

steps.description: A tinoridine-related anti-inflammatory program produced synthetic thienopyridines with unexpected antiplatelet and antithrombotic activity in rats; ticlopidine was selected.
The team synthesized and tested ticlopidine analogues to find improved activity and tolerability, yielding racemic PCR4099.
Separation of the racemate identified the active S-enantiomer, clopidogrel, which entered preclinical development.
The ADP-related platelet phenotype preceded molecular identification of P2Y12 as the target. Later receptor-null mouse experiments supported the link to clopidogrel.
Independently, investigators used weak P2T antagonist ATP as a starting point and modified its structure to generate potent nucleotide antagonists including AR-C69931MX, later known as cangrelor.

In the nucleotide-derived sequence, phosphate removal and core modifications produced a nonphosphate antagonist; further work to improve oral bioavailability led to ticagrelor, with a substantially changed architecture.

design.description: Researchers synthesized thienopyridine analogues, screened animal activity, selected a lead, and resolved a racemate to advance an active enantiomer with a more favorable experimental profile. Separately, nucleotide modifications improved stability, affinity and selectivity; later removal of phosphates and core changes created a different oral antagonist architecture.

circumstances.description: The anti-inflammatory analogue program and later analogue and enantiomer comparisons were planned; antiplatelet and antithrombotic activity in the original screen was unexpected.

limits: The assigned cohort member clopidogrel belongs to the thienopyridine branch, not the ATP-derived cangrelor/ticagrelor sequence. Both observed starting points are retained; multiple observation-led branches do not alone make the class mixed.

Ingall 1999 used the contemporary P2T receptor designation; the subsequent review supplies the link to P2Y12 and cangrelor. The first observation and priority of ATP antagonist activity were not independently reconstructed.
conflicts: S1 says none of the team's synthesized thienopyridines had anti-inflammatory or analgesic effects, whereas S5 describes anti-inflammatory activity in a combined thienopyridine/furopyridine series also tested for antiplatelet activity. Their exact compound sets and assays cannot be compared without the 1974 original; this possible series-level discrepancy remains unresolved and does not negate the reported antiplatelet observation.
gaps: The 1970s thienopyridine synthesis and animal-screen reports, including Podesta et al. 1974, were not read; the causal development narrative rests on the discoverer's retrospective S1.
Ingall 1999 was read at abstract extent only; the first observation of ATP antagonism was not independently reconstructed.

Hollopeter et al. 2001, DOI 10.1038/35051599, was located but not read in full; S4 acknowledges that earlier molecular-cloning report and supplies an independent primary experiment relevant to target identification.
